en: The Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra on the Great Expedient Means of the One Vehicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of Central India during the Song Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Merit of the Tathāgata’s True Meaning. Chapter One: The Merit of the Tathāgata’s True Meaning.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā, who had not long since placed their faith in the Dharma, said to one another:

“Lady Śrīmālā is my daughter; she is intelligent, of sharp faculties, quick-witted, and easy to enlighten. If she were to see the Buddha, she would surely understand the Dharma swiftly and her mind would be free from doubt.”
"It would be appropriate to send a messenger at this time to inspire his resolve for the Way. The lady replied,
"Now is precisely the right time."

The king and his consort wrote a letter to Śrīmālā, briefly extolling the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata. They then dispatched an attendant named Cāṇḍila to deliver the letter to the kingdom of Ayodhyā, where he entered the palace and respectfully presented it to Śrīmālā.

Having received the letter, Śrīmālā was filled with joy; she received it upon the crown of her head, recited it, and upheld it. Giving rise to a sense of rare wonder, she spoke these verses to Caṇḍīla:
"I have heard the voice of the Buddha, Unprecedented in this world;
That which he has spoken is true— I ought to cultivate offerings for him."
I look up with reverence to the Buddha, the World-Honored One!
You have appeared for the sake of the entire world;
may you likewise bestow your compassion and merciful pity, so that I may surely behold you.
As soon as this thought arose, the Buddha appeared in the sky;
emitting pure light everywhere, he revealed his peerless body.
Vaśitā and her retinue bowed their heads at his feet in prostration.
With minds entirely pure, they praised the Buddha’s true merits:
“The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body is peerless in the world;
Incomparable and inconceivable—therefore we now pay homage.”
The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so;
all phenomena are eternally abiding, therefore I take refuge in him.
Having subdued the faults of the mind, as well as the four types of faults of the body—
Having reached the stage that is difficult to subdue, I therefore pay homage to the Dharma King.
Knowing all *jñeya* (objects of knowledge), with mastery over the body of wisdom, you uphold all dharmas; for this reason, I now pay respectful homage.
Homage to you who transcend all measure; homage to you who are beyond comparison;
homage to you whose qualities are boundless; homage to you who are inconceivable.
Out of compassion, protect me and cause the seed of the Dharma to flourish.
"In this world and in future lives, may the Buddha always sustain you.
"I have long established you; you were already awakened in previous lives.
Now I sustain you again, and it shall be so in future births as well."
“I have already performed meritorious deeds in this present life and in other worlds;
may you, out of these roots of all such goodness, deign to accept me.”
At that time, Śrīmālā and her retinue prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet. Thereupon, amidst the assembly, the Buddha bestowed upon them this prediction:

“Because you have extolled the true merits of the Tathāgata, by virtue of these roots of goodness, for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas you shall be sovereign kings among devas and humans. In every place of birth, you shall always behold me and praise me in my presence, no different from how you do now.”

He shall again make offerings to immeasurable asaṃkhyeya buddhas, and after the passing of twenty thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he shall attain buddhahood, known by the name Samantaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

In that Buddha-land, there are no evil destinies, nor any sufferings of old age, illness, decay, affliction, or unpleasantness; furthermore, even the names of unwholesome and evil paths of action do not exist.

The physical form, strength, lifespan, and the various requisites for the five desires of the sentient beings in that land are all entirely joyful, surpassing those of the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
Those sentient beings are exclusively of the One Great Vehicle, and all sentient beings who have cultivated roots of goodness gather therein.

When Lady Śrīmālā received her prediction of enlightenment, immeasurable sentient beings—both devas and humans—aspired to be born in that land, and the World-Honored One predicted that they would all indeed attain rebirth there.
Chapter Two: The Ten Vows At that time, having heard her prediction of enlightenment, Śrīmālā stood with reverence and undertook the ten great vows, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a mind of transgression regarding the precepts I have received.
World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a mind of arrogance toward my elders and superiors."
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to a mind of anger toward any sentient being.
World-Honored One!”
"From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to thoughts of malice toward the physical forms of others or their external possessions.
World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not give rise to thoughts of stinginess regarding internal or external phenomena."
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until I attain bodhi, I shall not accept or store wealth and goods for my own sake; whatever I may receive, I shall do so entirely for the purpose of bringing poor and suffering sentient beings to maturity.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall not practice the four means of attraction for my own sake, but for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall gather in and sustain them with a mind free from attachment, a mind free from satiety, and a mind free from obstruction.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forth until I attain bodhi, if I see sentient beings who are solitary, imprisoned, ill, or afflicted by various calamities and hardships, I shall never abandon them even for a moment. I must bring them peace and security, benefiting them with righteous means to free them from all suffering, and only then shall I leave them.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, if I see those who capture and raise animals for slaughter—those of evil discipline—or those who violate the precepts, I shall never abandon them.”
When I have attained power, wherever I see these sentient beings, I shall subdue those who should be subdued and gather in those who should be gathered in.
Why is this? It is because through subduing and gathering [disciples], the Dharma is made to endure for a long time.

When the Dharma endures for a long time, devas and humans flourish, the evil realms diminish, and one is able to follow and turn the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata. Seeing these benefits, he rescues and gathers them, never abandoning them.
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until I attain bodhi, I shall uphold the true Dharma and never forget it. Why is this?
One who forgets the Dharma forgets the Mahāyāna; one who forgets the Mahāyāna forgets the pāramitās; and one who forgets the pāramitās has no desire for the Mahāyāna.

If a bodhisattva is not resolute regarding the Mahāyāna, they will be unable to attain the aspiration to embrace the true Dharma; consequently, regardless of where they enter according to their inclination, they will forever be incapable of transcending the stage of ordinary beings.

Having seen such immeasurable great faults, and having also seen the immeasurable benefits and merits for future bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who uphold the true Dharma, I have therefore accepted this great undertaking.
“Lord of Dharma, World-Honored One!
May you appear as my witness; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can directly perceive and know this.
For the roots of goodness of sentient beings are meager, or they may give rise to a web of doubt, because these ten great vows are exceedingly difficult to fulfill.”
They may, for a long night, suffer what is not meaningful or beneficial and fail to obtain peace and happiness.
For their sake, I now make this vow of truth before the Buddha:

"If I accept these ten great precepts and practice according to what I have said, by virtue of this vow, let celestial flowers rain down and celestial wondrous sounds resound within this great assembly."
When these words were spoken, a rain of various heavenly flowers fell from the void, and a wondrous voice proclaimed:
"So it is, so it is! What you have said is true and not otherwise."
Upon seeing those exquisite flowers and hearing those sounds, all doubts and perplexities within the entire assembly were completely dispelled. Rejoicing immeasurably, they made this vow:
"May we always be together with Śrīmālā, sharing in her conduct."
The World-Honored One granted the prediction of fulfillment for all the great assembly according to their respective wishes.
Chapter Three: The Three Great Vows. At that time, Śrīmālā again made three great vows before the Buddha, saying:

"By means of these true vows, may immeasurable and boundless sentient beings find peace and security; by means of these roots of goodness, may I attain the wisdom of the True Dharma in every birth—this is called the first great vow."
"Once I have attained the wisdom of the True Dharma, I shall preach it for the sake of sentient beings with an insatiable mind; this is called the second great vow.
Regarding the upholding of the True Dharma, I shall sacrifice my body, life, and wealth to protect and maintain the True Dharma; this is called the third great vow."
At that time, the World-Honored One then certified Śrīmālā’s three great vows, saying:

"Just as all forms are entirely contained within the realm of space, so too do the sands-of-the-Ganges vows of Bodhisattvas all enter into these three great vows; these three vows are truly vast and great."
Chapter Four: On Embracing [the Teachings] At that time, Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I shall now, further relying upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, speak of the true and non-differentiated nature of the great vows for subduing [the mind].”
The Buddha said to Śrīmālā,
“I grant you leave to speak as you wish.
Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha:
"All the vows of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are entirely contained within one great vow, namely, the upholding of the True Dharma.
To uphold the True Dharma is truly the Great Vow."
The Buddha praised Śrīmālā:
“Excellent, excellent!

Your wisdom and skillful means are profoundly deep and subtle. You have planted various roots of goodness throughout the long night; only those sentient beings of future ages who have long cultivated roots of goodness will be able to understand what you have said.”

What you have spoken regarding the upholding of the true Dharma is that which has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, present, and future—those who have taught it, those who are teaching it now, and those who will teach it in the future.
Now that I have attained unsurpassed enlightenment, I likewise constantly proclaim this upholding of the true Dharma. Thus I say:
"The merit inherent in upholding the true Dharma has no limit; the wisdom and eloquence of the Tathāgata are likewise without limit."
"Why is this? Because the upholding of the true Dharma possesses great merit and great benefit.
Thus did Śrīmālā address the Buddha.
"I shall, by relying on the Buddha's spiritual power, further expound the vast meaning of embracing the True Dharma.
The Buddha said, "Speak then."
Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha:
“The vast meaning of upholding the True Dharma is immeasurable; it attains all Buddha-dharmas and encompasses the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates.”
For example, when the kalpa first begins to form, great clouds arise everywhere, raining down rain of various colors and diverse jewels.
In this same way, the upholding of the True Dharma rains down immeasurable rewards of merit and the rain of immeasurable roots of goodness.
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, it is like when the kalpa first begins to form, there is a great mass of water that gives rise to the treasury of the trichiliocosm and four hundred billion kinds of various continents.”
Thus, by upholding the true Dharma, one gives rise to the immeasurable treasury of realms of the Mahāyāna:
the supernormal powers of all bodhisattvas;
and the peace, security, and happiness of all worlds.
All that is sovereign and at will within the mundane world,
as well as the formation of the kalpa of peace and bliss in the supramundane realm— even those things never before attained by devas and humans— all emerge from within it.
"Furthermore, it is like the great earth which bears four heavy burdens. What are these four?
First, the great oceans; second, the various mountains; third, the grasses and trees; and fourth, sentient beings."
In this way, sons and daughters of good family who embrace the True Dharma establish the great earth and are capable of bearing its fourfold heavy responsibilities; they are like that very earth.
What are these four? They are:
maturing those sentient beings who lack virtuous friends and have not heard the Dharma by means of the roots of goodness of humans and devas;
and bestowing the Śrāvaka Vehicle upon those who seek the Śrāvaka path.
To those who seek the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, he bestows the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
to those who seek the Mahāyāna, he bestows the Mahāyāna.
This is called the establishment of the great earth by sons and daughters of good family who embrace the true Dharma, and their capacity to bear the four kinds of heavy responsibilities.
World-Honored One!

Sons and daughters of good family who thus uphold the True Dharma establish the great earth; they are capable of bearing the four kinds of heavy responsibilities, acting as uninvited friends to all sentient beings, comforting and pitying them with great compassion, and serving as the mother of the world’s dharmas.
"Furthermore, it is like the great earth, which has four kinds of treasure stores.

What are these four? First, those of priceless value; second, those of superior value; third, those of middling value; and fourth, those of inferior value. These are called the four kinds of treasure stores of the great earth."
In this way, sons and daughters of good family who embrace the True Dharma establish the great earth and obtain four kinds of supreme great jewels among sentient beings. What are these four?
To those sons and daughters of good family who uphold the True Dharma, they grant the roots of goodness of the merits of humans and devas to those sentient beings who have not heard the non-Dharma;
to those who seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas, they grant the Śrāvaka-yāna;
and to those who seek the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, they grant the Pratyekabuddha-yāna.
To those who seek the Mahāyāna, one bestows the Mahāyāna.
Thus, sentient beings who obtain such great jewels all derive these extraordinary and rare merits from being sustained by sons and daughters of good family who uphold the True Dharma.
"Bhagavān! That which is called the 'Great Treasure Store' is precisely the upholding of the True Dharma. Bhagavān!"
To uphold the true Dharma—those who uphold the true Dharma do not see any difference between the true Dharma and upholding the true Dharma; the true Dharma itself is the upholding of the true Dharma.
World-Honored One!
There is no difference between the pāramitās and the upholding of the true Dharma; the upholding of the true Dharma is itself the pāramitā. Why is this?

Good sons and good daughters who uphold the True Dharma should bring to maturity through giving those who are to be matured by giving; they should even bring them to maturity by sacrificing their own limbs and members to protect their minds.
When those beings whom he has brought to maturity are established in the True Dharma, this is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

As for those who should be matured through ethical discipline (*śīla*), he matures them by guarding the six sense faculties, purifying the actions of body, speech, and mind, and even maintaining the four correct modes of deportment, thereby protecting their intentions.
To establish the True Dharma for those sentient beings whom one has brought to maturity is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).

Regarding those who should be matured through patience: if those sentient beings should revile, insult, slander, or intimidate one, one should—with a mind free from malice and with a mind intent on their benefit—employ the supreme power of patience, such that even one’s facial expression remains unchanged; thus, by protecting their minds, one brings them to maturity.
Establishing the True Dharma for those sentient beings whom he has brought to maturity is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Regarding those who should be matured through diligence, he does not give rise to a mind of indolence toward those sentient beings; rather, he generates a mind of great aspiration and supreme diligence. Even in his four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*), he protects their minds and brings them to maturity.
The establishment of the True Dharma for those sentient beings whom he has brought to maturity is called the *vīryapāramitā*.

"Those who should be matured through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*"): toward those sentient beings, with an undistracted mind and a non-outward-turned mind, possessing supreme right mindfulness such that what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago is never forgotten, he protects their intentions and brings them to maturity.
The establishment of the True Dharma for those sentient beings whom he has brought to maturity is called the perfection of dhyāna (dhyānapāramitā).

"Those who should be matured through wisdom: when those sentient beings inquire about all meanings, he expounds them with a fearless mind; regarding all treatises, all crafts, the ultimate fields of knowledge, and even various manual arts and affairs, he brings them to maturity while protecting their inclinations."
The establishment of the True Dharma by those beings whom he has brought to maturity is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Therefore, World-Honored One, there is no difference between the perfections and the embracing of the True Dharma; the embracing of the True Dharma is itself the perfection.
“World-Honored One!
Now, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall further expound upon the great meaning.
The Buddha said:
"Speak then. Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha:
"The upholding of the true Dharma and the one who upholds the true Dharma are not different; the upholding of the true Dharma and the one who upholds the true Dharma are not distinct."
A son or daughter of good family who upholds the true Dharma is, in fact, upholding the true Dharma. Why is this?
If a son or daughter of good family who upholds the true Dharma, for the sake of upholding the true Dharma, relinquishes the three types of attachments.
What are the three? They are:
body, life, and wealth.

When good sons and good daughters relinquish their bodies, they will reach the ultimate limit of birth and death, becoming free from old age, illness, and death, and attain the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body—a body that is indestructible, eternally abiding, immutable, and inconceivable in its merit.

Those who have relinquished their lives attain equality with the ultimate limit of birth and death; they are forever free from death, obtaining boundless, eternally abiding, and inconceivable merit, and they penetrate all the most profound Buddha-dharmas.

Regarding the relinquishing of wealth: it is equal to the ultimate limit of birth and death; it attains merits that are not shared with any sentient beings, which are inexhaustible, undiminishing, eternally abiding, and inconceivable; and it receives the most excellent offerings from all sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!

Such sons and daughters of good family who relinquish these three parts and embrace the True Dharma will always receive the prediction of all Buddhas and be gazed upon with reverence by all sentient beings.”
“World-Honored One!

Furthermore, when the True Dharma is about to perish, those sons and daughters of good family who uphold the True Dharma will find that monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen form factions, engage in disputes, and cause destruction and dissension.”

By being free from flattery, free from deception, and free from artifice, one comes to love and delight in the true Dharma, upholds the true Dharma, and enters the circle of those who follow the Dharma.
Those who enter the circle of those who follow the Dharma will certainly receive a prophecy of enlightenment from all the Buddhas.
"World-Honored One!

I see that the upholding of the true Dharma possesses such great power; the Buddha is the true eye and true wisdom, the root of the Dharma, the one who has attained penetration of the Dharma, and the refuge of the true Dharma—this he knows and sees in its entirety."
At that time, the World-Honored One, regarding the great power of diligence in upholding the True Dharma as spoken by Śrīmālā, gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, saying: "So it is, Śrīmālā!"
It is as you have said.
The power of great diligence in upholding the True Dharma is such that, O Śrīmālā, it is like a strong man who, when his body is touched even slightly, experiences intense pain.
Thus it is, Śrīmālā!
To slightly embrace the true Dharma causes Māra to suffer and be distressed;
I do not see any other single wholesome dharma that causes Māra such grief and distress as does the slight embracing of the true Dharma.
Furthermore, just as a bull king is incomparable in form and color, surpassing all other oxen;
so too, even a small amount of the correct Dharma embraced by the Mahāyāna surpasses all the roots of goodness of the two vehicles, because it is vast.
Furthermore, just as Sumeru, the king of mountains, is majestic and extraordinary, surpassing all other mountains;

so too does the Mahāyāna—by relinquishing body, life, and wealth with a mind of gathering to embrace the True Dharma—surpass all roots of goodness of those who have newly entered the Mahāyāna but do not relinquish body, life, and wealth, let alone those of the Two Vehicles.
Because it is vast and great.
Therefore, Śrīmālā, you should,
by means of upholding the True Dharma, reveal it to sentient beings, instruct sentient beings, and establish sentient beings.
Thus it is, Śrīmālā!
The upholding of the true Dharma brings such great benefit, such great merit, and such great fruit. Śrīmālā!
For incalculable upon incalculable eons, I have said:
"The merit and benefits of upholding the True Dharma cannot reach their limit.
Therefore, upholding the True Dharma possesses immeasurable and boundless merit.
Chapter Five: The Single Vehicle. The Buddha said to Śrīmālā:
"Now you shall further expound upon the correct Dharma upheld by all Buddhas!"
Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That which upholds the True Dharma is the Mahāyāna.”
Why is this? World-Honored One, the Mahāyāna gives birth to all wholesome dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, the mundane, and the supramundane.
World-Honored One!
Just as the great lake Anavatapta gives rise to the eight great rivers,
so too does the Mahāyāna give birth to all wholesome dharmas— those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and those mundane and supramundane.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, just as all seeds depend upon the earth to grow,
so too do all the wholesome dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those of the mundane and supramundane realms depend upon the Mahāyāna to increase.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
To abide in the Great Vehicle and embrace the Great Vehicle is itself to abide in the two vehicles and embrace the two vehicles, as well as all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas.
"As the Blessed One has spoken of the six sense bases.
What are these six? Namely:"
The endurance of the True Dharma, the extinction of the True Dharma, the Prātimokṣa, the Vinaya, renunciation, and full ordination—
these six points are taught for the sake of the Mahāyāna.
Why is this? That which is the abiding of the True Dharma is for the sake of the Mahāyāna; thus, it is said that the abiding of the Mahāyāna is the abiding of the True Dharma.
That which is the extinction of the True Dharma is for the sake of the Mahāyāna; thus, it is said that the extinction of the Mahāyāna is the extinction of the True Dharma.
The two dharmas of *prātimokṣa* and *vinaya* are identical in meaning though different in name; *vinaya* is precisely the training of the Mahāyāna. Why is this so?

Because one goes forth and receives full ordination by relying on the Buddha, it is therefore said that the Mahāyāna rules of decorum and precepts constitute the Vinaya, the going forth, and the reception of full ordination.
Therefore, an Arhat does not go forth or receive full ordination.
Why is this? Because an Arhat goes forth and receives full ordination by relying upon the Tathāgata.
The Arhat takes refuge in the Buddha; the Arhat possesses fear. Why is this?

Because the Arhat dwells with a perception of dread toward all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), like a person who perceives someone brandishing a sword coming to harm him; therefore, the Arhat does not possess ultimate bliss.
For what reason?
World-Honored One,
that which relies does not seek a reliance.

Just as sentient beings, being without refuge, experience various terrors, and because of those terrors seek a refuge, so too does an Arhat have fear; because of that fear, he takes refuge in the Tathāgata.
“World-Honored One!
Arhats and pratyekabuddhas possess fear; therefore, for arhats and pratyekabuddhas, the phenomena of further birth are not exhausted, and thus there is birth;
their holy life is not fully accomplished, and thus it is not pure.”
Because affairs are not brought to completion, there must be that which is to be performed;
because one has not crossed over to the other shore, there must be that which is to be severed.
Because one does not sever [these], one remains far from the realm of nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha attains parinirvāṇa and accomplishes all meritorious qualities.
Therefore, arhats and pratyekabuddhas do not accomplish all meritorious qualities.
To speak of attaining *nirvāṇa* is the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*).
Only the Tathāgata attains *parinirvāṇa*, having accomplished immeasurable merit.
Therefore, because Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas accomplish only measurable merit, to say that they attain *nirvāṇa* is the Buddha’s skillful means.
Only the Tathāgata attains parinirvāṇa and accomplishes inconceivable merit.
Therefore, when it is said that arhats and pratyekabuddhas attain nirvāṇa by accomplishing conceivable merit, this is the Buddha’s skillful means.
Only the Tathāgata attains parinirvāṇa; having completely severed and extinguished all faults that ought to be abandoned, he achieves supreme purity.
Arhats and pratyekabuddhas still possess residual faults and are not supremely pure; therefore, their claim to have attained nirvāṇa is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddha.
Only the Tathāgata attains parinirvāṇa, being gazed upon by all sentient beings, and transcends the realms of arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.

Therefore, Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are far removed from the realm of Nirvāṇa. When it is said that Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, having observed the four ultimate knowledges of liberation, attain a place of rest, this too is a skillful means of the Tathāgata—a teaching of provisional meaning that is not yet definitive.
"Why is this? There are two kinds of death. What are these two?"
They are: death by fragmentation and inconceivable transformation-death.
Death by fragmentation refers to delusory sentient beings.
Inconceivable transformative death refers to the mind-made bodies of arhats,
pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of great power, up until the ultimate, unsurpassed enlightenment.
Among the two kinds of death, because it refers to the death of the segmented [body], it is said that for Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, "birth has been exhausted.
Because they have attained the realization of the fruit with remainder, it is said that "the holy life has been established.

Because they have severed the deceptive afflictions—which ordinary beings, humans, and devas cannot accomplish, and which the seven types of trainees had not previously performed—it is said that "what was to be done has been accomplished."
Because the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have severed the afflictions that would otherwise lead to further existence, it is said that they do not undergo future birth.
This does not mean they have exhausted all afflictions, nor has it been said that they have exhausted all modes of rebirth; therefore, it is said that they do not undergo future birth.
Why is this? There are afflictions that cannot be severed by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
"There are two kinds of afflictions."
What are these two? They are:
the afflictions of the abiding ground and the arising afflictions.
There are four kinds of abiding stages (bhūmi).
What are the four? They are as follows:
One perceives four abodes: the abode of views, the abode of desire-attachment, the abode of form-attachment, and the abode of attachment to existence.
These four types of abodes give rise to all active afflictions.
"O Bhagavat, that which arises is momentary mind associated with moments.
But the ground of abiding in beginningless ignorance is dissociated from the mind."
World-Honored One!

These four stages of abiding (*catur-vihāra-bhūmi*), which serve as the basis and seeds for all higher afflictions, cannot be compared to the stage of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) by means of calculation or analogy.
“World-Honored One!

Thus, as for the power of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), among the four grounds of abiding that are categorized under craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), the ground of abiding ignorance possesses the greatest power.

It is, for example, like the evil Māra Pāpīyas, who excels in physical form, strength, lifespan, retinue, requisites, and sovereignty within the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*”).

Thus, the power of the ground of abiding ignorance is the most supreme among the four grounds of abiding that comprise craving for existence; it serves as the basis for the afflictions numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges and also causes the four kinds of afflictions to endure for a long time.
That which cannot be severed by the wisdom of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, but can only be severed by the Bodhi-wisdom of the Tathāgata—
thus it is, World-Honored One!
The ground of abiding ignorance is the most powerful of all.
“World-Honored One! Just as the grasping (*upādāna*), conditioned by the cause of outflowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*), gives rise to the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*),

so too does the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), conditioned by the cause of non-outflowing karma (*anāsrava-karma*), give rise to the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of great power.”

In these three stages, the arising of those three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*) and the arising from untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) depend upon the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*); they have conditions and are not without conditions.
Therefore, the three kinds of mind-made bodies and untainted karma take the ground of the abiding of ignorance as their condition.
World-Honored One!

Thus, these four *bhūmis* of abiding in craving are not identical in their activity to the *bhūmi* of abiding in ignorance; the *bhūmi* of abiding in ignorance is distinct and separate from the four *bhūmis*.
These are severed at the stage of Buddhahood and severed by the wisdom of Buddha-enlightenment. Why is this?
Because Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, though they have severed the four kinds of abiding grounds, do not exhaust their outflows; they lack sovereign power and do not realize [the ultimate fruit].
That which is untainted yet not exhausted is precisely the ground of the abiding of ignorance.
"World-Honored One!

Because Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas in their final existence are shrouded and obstructed by the ground of the abiding of ignorance, they do not know and do not awaken to various dharmas."
Because of this lack of knowledge and vision, that which ought to be abandoned is not abandoned and is not brought to completion.
Because it is not abandoned, it is called liberation with residual faults, rather than liberation free from all faults;
it is called purity with residual impurities, rather than total purity.
This is called the accomplishment of remaining virtues, not of all virtues.

Because one has accomplished remaining liberation, remaining purity, and remaining virtues, one knows that there remains suffering to be known, that there remains the origin to be abandoned, that there remains cessation to be realized, and that there remains the path to be cultivated; this is called attaining a small portion of nirvana.
Those who have attained a small portion of *nirvāṇa* are said to be "heading toward the realm of *nirvāṇa*.

If one knows all suffering, abandons all its origin, realizes all its cessation, and cultivates the entire path, one attains the eternally abiding *nirvāṇa* within this impermanent, decaying world and this impermanent, diseased world;
and within this unprotected world and this world without refuge, one becomes a protector and a refuge.
Why is this? Because one attains nirvana because dharmas have no superiority or inferiority;
one attains nirvana because wisdom is equal.
Because liberation is equal, one attains nirvāṇa;
because purity is equal, one attains nirvāṇa.
Therefore, nirvāṇa is of a single flavor and an equal flavor, namely, the flavor of liberation.
“World-Honored One!
If the ground of the abiding of ignorance is neither severed nor brought to ultimate end, one cannot attain the single flavor, the flavor of the equality of clarity and liberation.”

Why is this? Because as long as the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is not severed and not brought to ultimate completion, the dharmas that ought to be severed—which exceed the sands of the Ganges in number—will likewise remain unsevered and incomplete. Because these dharmas exceeding the sands of the Ganges have not been severed, the dharmas exceeding the sands of the Ganges that ought to be attained will remain unattained, and those that ought to be realized will remain unrealized.
Therefore, the accumulated ground of the dwelling of ignorance gives rise to all afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as the higher afflictions.

It gives rise to the higher afflictions of mind, the higher afflictions of tranquility (*śamatha*), the higher afflictions of insight (*vipaśyanā*), the higher afflictions of dhyāna, the higher afflictions of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), the higher afflictions of skillful means (*upāya*), the higher afflictions of knowledge (*jñāna*), the higher afflictions of the fruit (*phala*), the higher afflictions of the [ten] powers (*bala*), and the higher afflictions of the [four] fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Such higher afflictions, exceeding the sands of the Ganges in number, are severed by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom.

All things are established based upon the ground of abiding ignorance; all higher afflictions arise because they are caused by the ground of abiding ignorance and conditioned by the ground of abiding ignorance.
“World-Honored One!
In this arising of afflictions, the mind and its moments are associated moment by moment;
World-Honored One!”
The ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), which is dissociated from the mind and beginningless.
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, all those dharmas to be abandoned by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom that exceed the sands of the Ganges are all sustained and established by this ground of abiding ignorance.”
For example, just as all seeds depend upon the earth for their production, establishment, and growth— and if the earth is destroyed, they are likewise destroyed— so too,

all those dharmas that are to be abandoned by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom, which exceed the sands of the Ganges in number, depend upon the ground of the abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) for their production,

establishment, and growth; if the ground of the abiding ignorance is severed, all those dharmas to be abandoned by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom, exceeding the sands of the Ganges, are likewise severed.

Thus, having severed all afflictions and secondary afflictions, one attains all dharmas realized by the Tathāgatas—which exceed the sands of the Ganges—in an unimpeded penetration of all knowledge and vision, remaining free from all faults and evils, and acquiring all merits.
The Dharma King and Lord of Dharma has attained mastery and ascended to the stage of sovereignty over all dharmas.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha lets out a true lion’s roar:
"Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence."
"Therefore, the World-Honored One, relying on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), has given a categorical declaration with the lion's roar:
'World-Honored One!
There are two kinds of knowledge regarding the non-existence of further existence (*anupādadāna-punarbhava-jñāna*).'"
That is to say:
the Tathāgata, through supreme mastery, has subdued the four māras, emerged from all worlds, is gazed upon by all sentient beings, and has attained the inconceivable Dharma-body.
Having attained unimpeded mastery over all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) on these stages, there is nothing further to be done above them.

On this stage of non-attainment, he is courageous through the ten powers; ascending to the foremost, unsurpassed stage of fearlessness, his unimpeded wisdom-contemplation regarding all objects of knowledge is not dependent on others, and he utters the lion’s roar of the knowledge that there is no further rebirth.
“World-Honored One!
Arhats and pratyekabuddhas have crossed over the fear of birth and death and have attained the bliss of liberation in succession, thinking thus:
‘I am free from the terror of birth and death, and I shall no longer undergo the suffering of birth and death.’”
"World-Honored One!
When Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas observe in this way, they attain the state of no further rebirth and contemplate the ground of Nirvana, the supreme place of rest."
World-Honored One!

Regarding that ground previously attained, he is not deluded about the Dharma and does not rely on others; he also knows for himself that there remains further ground to be traversed, and that he will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas both enter the Mahāyāna; the Mahāyāna is itself the Buddha-vehicle. Therefore, the three vehicles are in fact the one vehicle.

Those who attain the One Vehicle attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is itself the realm of *nirvāṇa*; the realm of *nirvāṇa* is itself the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata. Those who attain the ultimate *dharmakāya* have attained the ultimate One Vehicle; there is no difference between the Tathāgata and the *dharmakāya*, for the Tathāgata is the *dharmakāya*.
Those who attain the ultimate *dharmakāya* have attained the ultimate One Vehicle; "ultimate" means that which is boundless and uninterrupted.
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata does not abide for a limited duration; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, abides equally throughout the future limit.
The Tathāgata’s great compassion is without limit, and his consolation of the world is likewise without limit.”
One who speaks thus—that the Tathāgata possesses infinite great compassion and infinitely comforts the world—is called one who rightly speaks of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, if one says that he is the inexhaustible Dharma, the eternally abiding Dharma, and the refuge for all the world, this too is called rightly speaking of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, for those in the world who have not yet crossed over and for the world that is without refuge, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is the inexhaustible refuge and the eternally abiding refuge, equal to the limit of the future.
"The Dharma refers to the teaching of the Single Vehicle (ekayāna), and the Sangha refers to the assembly of the Three Vehicles.
These two refuges are not ultimate refuges; they are called 'partial refuges.'"
Why is this? Because when the Dharma of the One Vehicle path is taught, one attains the ultimate Dharmakāya; beyond this, there is no further teaching of a Dharmakāya of the One Vehicle.

Those belonging to the assembly of the Three Vehicles experience fear and dread; they take refuge in the Tathāgata, seeking liberation through practice and training toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, these two types of reliance are not ultimate reliances; they are limited reliances.

“If there are sentient beings whom the Tathāgata has subdued, who take refuge in the Tathāgata and receive the nourishment of the Dharma, and give rise to a mind of faith and joy to take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha—these two refuges are not [the ultimate];
it is taking refuge in the Tathāgata that is the true refuge.”
To take refuge in the ultimate truth is to take refuge in the Tathāgata.
These two refuges in the ultimate truth constitute the final refuge in the Tathāgata. Why is this so?
The Tathāgata is not different; the two refuges are not different.
The Tathāgata is itself the three refuges. Why is this?
He teaches the path of the One Vehicle.

With the lion’s roar of one who has accomplished the four fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata, he speaks; if the Tathāgata teaches through skillful means according to their inclinations, that is itself the Mahāyāna, and there are no three vehicles.
The three vehicles enter into the One Vehicle; the One Vehicle is precisely the vehicle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Chapter Six: The Infinite Noble Truths. "World-Honored One!
When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas first contemplate the Noble Truths, they sever all the stages of abiding with a single wisdom;
with that same single wisdom, they achieve the fourfold severance, knowledge, merit, and realization, and they also skillfully understand the meaning of these four dharmas.
World-Honored One!

There is no supramundane, most excellent wisdom that arrives gradually through the four knowledges or that arrives gradually through the four conditions; the dharma that is free from gradual arrival is supramundane, most excellent wisdom.
“World-Honored One!
That which is like a diamond is the wisdom of the primary meaning.
World-Honored One!”
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not sever the ground of the abiding of ignorance; the knowledge of the first noble truth is the knowledge of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
Blessed One, it is by means of the non-dual knowledge of the noble truths that one severs all the grounds of abiding.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is not within the realm of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
His inconceivable wisdom of emptiness severs the storehouse of all afflictions.
“World-Honored One!
If one destroys the storehouse of all afflictions through ultimate knowledge, this is called the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
The knowledge of the first noble truth is not ultimate knowledge; it is the knowledge that leads toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
“World-Honored One!

‘Noble meaning’ does not refer to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas accomplish only limited merit, and because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas accomplish only a small portion of merit, they are called ‘noble.’”
"O World-Honored One, the Noble Truths are not the truths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
nor are they the merits of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

This truth was first realized by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; he subsequently revealed and expounded it for the world that is enclosed within the shell of ignorance. For this reason, it is called a Noble Truth.
Chapter Seven: The Tathāgatagarbha "Regarding the Noble Truths: they proclaim a profound meaning that is subtle and difficult to know, lying beyond the sphere of discursive thought."
This is known by the wise, yet it cannot be believed by anyone in the world.
Why is this? Because this teaching is the profoundly deep Tathāgatagarbha.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the realm of the Tathāgatas; it is not something known by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
It is within the locus of the Tathāgatagarbha that the meaning of the Noble Truths is explained.

Because the locus of the Tathāgatagarbha is profoundly deep, the Noble Truths are likewise said to be profound; they are subtle and difficult to know, beyond the sphere of discursive thought, known only by the wise, and cannot be believed by the entire world.

Chapter Eight: On the Dharma-body "If one has no doubt regarding the Tathāgatagarbha, which is enveloped by immeasurable stores of afflictions, one will likewise have no doubt regarding the Dharmakāya, which emerges from those immeasurable stores of afflictions."

Those who attain certainty of mind regarding the teaching on the Tathāgatagarbha, the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, the inconceivable realm of the Buddha, and its skillful exposition, are those who believe in and understand the two noble truths.
That which is thus difficult to know and difficult to understand refers to the teaching on the meaning of the two noble truths.
What is the teaching on the meaning of the two noble truths?
It is the teaching on the meaning of the noble truth of conditioned activity and the teaching on the meaning of the noble truth of unconditioned non-activity.
To explain the meaning of the Noble Truths as being "produced" is to speak of the four Noble Truths as having a limited measure. Why is this?
It is not through another that one can know all suffering, abandon all origination, realize all cessation, and cultivate all paths.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
There is conditioned birth-and-death and unconditioned birth-and-death.
Nirvāṇa is likewise: there is that with remainder and that without remainder.
To explain the meaning of the noble truth of non-action is to explain the meaning of the immeasurable four noble truths. Why is this?

Because one is able, by means of one's own power, to know all suffering, to sever the accumulation of all [suffering], to realize the cessation of all [suffering], and to cultivate the path leading to the cessation of all [suffering].
Regarding these eight noble truths, the Tathāgata has taught them as the four noble truths.
Thus, the meaning of these four noble truths of non-action is fully realized only by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is not fully realized by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? Nirvana is not attained through inferior, middling, or superior dharmas. Why is this?

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has reached the ultimate consummation regarding the meaning and substance of the four noble truths of non-action; for he, as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows all future suffering, abandons all accumulation comprised of primary and secondary afflictions, extinguishes all mind-born bodies, and realizes the cessation that is the eradication of all suffering.
“World-Honored One!
It is not because of the destruction of phenomena that it is called the cessation of suffering.

What is called the cessation of suffering is named as being without beginning and without action, without arising and without exhaustion, eternally abiding apart from exhaustion, pure by its own nature, and free from the storehouse of all afflictions.”
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is said to be the accomplishment of Buddha-dharmas that surpass the sands of the Ganges—dharmas that are inseparable, non-detached, non-different, and inconceivable.
“World-Honored One!
Thus, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, when not separated from the storehouse of afflictions (*kleśakośa*), is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Chapter Nine: The Meaning of Emptiness Concealing Reality. “World-Honored One!”
The wisdom of the Tathāgatagarbha is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of emptiness.
World-Honored One!
This Tathāgatagarbha has never been seen and has never been attained by any Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas of great power.
“World-Honored One!
There are two kinds of wisdom regarding the emptiness of the Tathāgatagarbha.
World-Honored One!”
The empty tathāgatagarbha is that which is separated from, liberated from, or distinct from the storehouse of all afflictions.
World-Honored One,
the non-empty tathāgatagarbha consists of the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, which are not separated from, not liberated from, and not distinct [from it].
World-Honored One!
Regarding these two types of wisdom of emptiness, the great śrāvakas are able to have faith in the Tathāgata’s [wisdom].
As for the wisdom of emptiness of all arhats and pratyekabuddhas, it functions within the sphere of the four non-erroneous [realities].
Therefore, all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have never seen this before, nor have they ever attained it.
The cessation of all suffering is realized only by the Buddha, who destroys the storehouse of all afflictions and cultivates the path that extinguishes all suffering.
Chapter Ten: The Chapter on the Single Truth “World-Honored One!
Of these Four Noble Truths, three are impermanent and one is permanent. Why is this so?”
The three truths enter into the characteristics of the conditioned; that which enters into the characteristics of the conditioned is impermanent.
That which is impermanent is a false and illusory dharma.
A false and illusory dharma is not a truth, is not permanent, and is not a refuge.
Therefore, the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, and the truth of the path are not the ultimate truth; they are impermanent and not a refuge.
Chapter Eleven: The Single Refuge. "The single truth of the cessation of suffering is free from conditioned characteristics; that which is free from conditioned characteristics is permanent."
That which is permanent is not a deceptive phenomenon.
That which is not a deceptive phenomenon is the truth, the permanent, and the refuge.
Therefore, the Truth of Cessation is the ultimate reality.

Chapter Twelve: On Perversion and Reality "The inconceivable is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); it transcends the objects of perception of the mind and consciousness of all sentient beings, and it is not within the sphere of wisdom of any Arhat or Pratyekabuddha."
For example, one born blind cannot see various forms, and a seven-day-old infant cannot see the sun’s orb.
The Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is likewise:
it is not an object of perception for the mental consciousness of any ordinary person, nor is it the sphere of wisdom for those of the two vehicles.
The consciousness of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) is inverted by the two views;
the wisdom of all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, however, is pure. Regarding the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*):

when ordinary persons, regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), give rise to the view of self, false conceptualization, and attachment, they produce two views; these are called the view of extremes, namely, the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) and the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
To see all conditioned phenomena as impermanent is the view of annihilationism, not the correct view;
to see nirvana as permanent is the view of eternalism, not the correct view.
Such views are produced through the perception of false conceptualization.

By analyzing and reflecting upon the various faculties of the body, one perceives their disintegration in the present life but fails to see their continuity in existence; thus, due to false conceptualization, one gives rise to the view of annihilationism.

Being ignorant and deluded regarding the continuity of the mind, failing to understand or know the objective realm of consciousness within a single moment, one gives rise to the view of eternalism due to false conceptualization.
This false conceptualization, regarding that object, either exceeds or falls short of it, giving rise to divergent thoughts and discriminations such as annihilationism or eternalism.
Deluded sentient beings, with respect to the five aggregates of clinging, perceive permanence in the impermanent, pleasure in suffering, self in the non-self, and purity in the impure.
The pure wisdom of all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas has, from the very beginning, never perceived the realm of omniscience or the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.

"There may be sentient beings who, because they believe the Buddha’s words, give rise to the perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, the perception of self, and the perception of purity; these are not inverted views, and are called right view."
Why is this? Because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is the perfection of permanence, the perfection of bliss, the perfection of self, and the perfection of purity.
To perceive the Buddha’s Dharma-body in this way is called right view.

"One who possesses right view is a true child of the Buddha; born from the mouth of the Buddha, born from the True Dharma, and born through transformation by the Dharma, they have obtained the remaining wealth of the Dharma.
World-Honored One!"

Regarding "pure wisdom": it refers to the perfection of wisdom of all arhats and pratyekabuddhas. Although this is called pure wisdom, even with respect to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), it is not yet its domain; how much less so for the wisdom of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*)?
Why is this? Those who have begun their practice in the three vehicles are not deluded regarding the Dharma.
They should awaken to and attain its meaning; for their sake, the World-Honored One has taught the four reliances.
World-Honored One!
These four reliances are worldly dharmas.
World-Honored One!
The one basis refers to the basis of all things, the supramundane, supreme, ultimate basis, namely, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Chapter Thirteen: On Innate Purity. "World-Honored One!..."
Birth and death depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*; because of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is said that the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is unknowable.
World-Honored One, that birth and death are spoken of because there is the *tathāgatagarbha*—this is called a well-spoken teaching.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding birth-and-death: birth-and-death consists in the dissolution of the faculties of sensation, followed by the successive arising of the faculties of sensation; this is called birth-and-death, World-Honored One.”
Regarding birth and death, these two phenomena are the Tathāgatagarbha.

It is only through worldly convention that there is death and birth; "death" refers to the destruction of the sense faculties, and "birth" refers to the arising of new sense faculties. The Tathāgatagarbha itself has neither birth nor death.
The Tathāgatagarbha is free from the characteristics of the conditioned; the Tathāgatagarbha is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Therefore, the Tathāgatagarbha is the support, the sustenance, and the foundation.
World-Honored One!
The Buddha-dharmas are not separate, not severed, not detached, not different, and inconceivable.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatagarbha is that which serves as the support, sustenance, and foundation for conditioned phenomena external to it— those which are severed and detached.
"World-Honored One, if there were no Tathāgatagarbha, one would not feel weary of suffering nor seek to attain Nirvāṇa."

Why is this? Because regarding these six consciousnesses and the knowledge of mental factors—these seven phenomena do not abide for even a moment; they do not plant manifold sufferings, nor can one become weary of suffering or joyfully seek nirvana through them.
World-Honored One!

The Tathāgatagarbha has no beginning; it is a dharma that neither arises nor ceases, yet it gives rise to all forms of suffering, leading one to become weary of suffering and to joyfully seek nirvāṇa.
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatagarbha is not the self, not a sentient being, not a life-principle, and not a person.
The Tathāgatagarbha is not within the realm of sentient beings who hold views of a personal body, who are subject to inversions, or whose minds are distracted by emptiness.”
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatagarbha is the treasury of the Dharma-realm, the treasury of the Dharma-body, the supreme supramundane treasury, and the treasury of intrinsic purity.”
This nature, the Tathāgatagarbha which is inherently pure, is defiled by adventitious afflictions and secondary afflictions; it is the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata. Why is this so?
A momentary wholesome mind is not defiled by afflictions;
a momentary unwholesome mind is likewise not defiled by afflictions.
Afflictions do not touch the mind, and the mind does not touch afflictions. How can a mind that does not touch [afflictions] become defiled?
World-Honored One!
Yet there are afflictions, and there is the defilement of the mind by afflictions; that the intrinsically pure mind can be defiled is difficult to comprehend.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, [can fully understand this].
“True eye and true wisdom are the root of the Dharma, the penetration of the Dharma, and the reliance of the True Dharma; they constitute knowing and seeing according to reality.
When Queen Śrīmālā spoke these difficult-to-understand teachings and questioned the Buddha, the Buddha immediately expressed his approval: “So it is, so it is!”
That the mind, which is pure by nature, can yet be defiled is difficult to comprehend.

There are two things that are difficult to comprehend: namely, that the mind is pure by nature is difficult to comprehend, and that this very mind is defiled by afflictions is likewise difficult to comprehend.
These two dharmas can be heard and received by you and by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished the Great Dharma; as for all other śrāvakas, they can only believe in the words of the Buddha.

Chapter Fourteen: On the True Disciple (Tathāgata-putra) "If my disciples follow through faith as their predominant faculty, having relied upon clear understanding, they accord with the knowledge of the Dharma and thereby attain the ultimate."
One who possesses knowledge that accords with the Dharma observes the conceptual designations of the faculties and the objects of mental resolve;
observes karmic retribution;
and observes the eye of the Arhat.
One contemplates the bliss of mastery over the mind and the bliss of dhyāna;
one contemplates the noble supernormal powers of mastery belonging to arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of great power.
These are the accomplishments of the five kinds of skillful means of contemplation.

In the future world after my parinirvāṇa, my disciples who follow through faith and with superior resolve, relying on clear faith and conforming to the knowledge of the Dharma, will attain ultimate realization regarding the intrinsically pure mind that has been defiled by afflictions; this ultimate realization is the cause for entering the path of the Mahāyāna.
"One who has faith in the Tathāgata possesses such great benefit as not to slander the profound meaning.
At that time, Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"There are further great benefits; I shall now rely upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power to speak of this meaning once more."
The Buddha said, “Speak further.
Śrīmālā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“There are three kinds of sons and daughters of good family who, regarding this profound meaning, remain free from self-injury, give rise to great merit, and enter the path of the Mahāyāna.
What are these three?
That is to say:
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family personally accomplishes the profound knowledge of the Dharma;
or if a son of good family or a daughter of good family accomplishes the knowledge of the Dharma that accords with reality.

If good sons or good daughters do not personally understand these profound dharmas, they should look up to the World-Honored One, thinking: "This is not within my realm; it is known only by the Buddha."
This is called the way in which good sons and good daughters look up to and rely upon the Tathāgata. Excluding these good sons and good daughters,

as for all other sentient beings who stubbornly cling to false teachings regarding the profound dharmas, who oppose the true Dharma, and who cultivate the rotten seeds of various non-Buddhist paths— they shall be subdued by the power of the king, as well as by the powers of devas, nāgas, and spirits.
At that time, Śrīmālā and her retinue prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent!”

"Śrīmālā! You have skillfully guarded the profound Dharma and subdued what is not the Dharma with perfect appropriateness; having personally attended hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas, you are able to explain this meaning."

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a supreme radiance that illuminated the entire assembly; his body ascended into the air to a height of seven tala trees, and walking through the sky, he returned to Śrāvastī.
At that time, Queen Śrīmālā and her retinue joined their palms toward the Buddha, gazing at him with insatiable devotion, their eyes never wavering for a moment.

Once he had passed beyond the range of their vision, they leaped for joy and, each praising the merits of the Tathāgata, remained fully mindful of the Buddha as they returned to the city to praise the Mahāyāna to King Amitāyus.
The women in the city who were seven years of age or older were converted to the Mahāyāna.
The friend, addressing the Great King, likewise converted all the men who were seven years of age or older to the Mahāyāna; thus, the people of the entire nation turned toward the Mahāyāna.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Jeta Grove and addressed the Elder Ānanda, instructing him to call to mind Śakra, Lord of the Devas. Immediately, Śakra and his retinue suddenly arrived and stood before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded this sutra to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Elder Ānanda.
Having finished speaking, he addressed Śakra, saying:
"You should receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra."

Kauśika! If a son or daughter of good family were to cultivate the practices for enlightenment and practice the six pāramitās for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges, yet another son or daughter of good family were to hear, receive, read, recite, or even uphold this sūtra scroll, their merit would be far greater than that; how much more so if they were to explain it extensively for others?
"Therefore, Kauśika, you should read and recite this sutra, and explain it in detail for the sake of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He further addressed Ānanda:
“You, too, should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and explain it extensively for the fourfold assembly.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What shall this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Śakra:
"This sutra accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit; all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to fully observe, know, or see it. Kausika!"

You should know that this sutra is a profound, subtle, and magnificent mass of great merit; I shall now briefly state its name for you—listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
The Buddha said:
"This sutra is 'Praising the Tathāgata’s True and Supreme Merit'; it should be upheld as such.
It is 'The Inconceivable Great Acceptance'; it should be upheld as such."
"Compendium of All Vows," thus one should uphold it.
"The Exposition of the Inconceivable Embracing of the True Dharma," thus one should uphold it.
"Explaining the entry into the One Vehicle"—thus should it be upheld.
"Explaining the boundless Noble Truths"—thus should it be upheld.
"Explaining the Tathāgatagarbha"—thus should it be upheld.
"Explaining the Dharma-body"—thus should it be upheld.
"Explaining that the meaning of emptiness conceals the reality"—thus should it be upheld.
"Explaining the single truth"—thus should it be upheld.
"Proclaiming the eternal, peaceful, and singular refuge"—thus should it be upheld.
"Proclaiming the reality of what is inverted"—thus should it be upheld.
"Proclaiming the concealment of the intrinsically pure mind"—thus should it be upheld.
"Recite it as 'The Exposition of the True Son of the Tathāgata'—thus should you uphold it.
Recite it as 'The Lion’s Roar of Queen Śrīmālā'—thus should you uphold it.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!"
This sutra expounds the severing of all doubts, definitively establishing the ultimate meaning and entry into the path of the One Vehicle. Kausika!
I now entrust this *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* to you; until the Dharma remains, you should uphold, recite, and extensively explain it in detail.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! I receive the Honored One’s instruction upon the crown of my head."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, the Venerable Ānanda, and the entire great assembly—including devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

I vow to serve and honor the *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahopāya-vaipulya-sūtra*, as well as my ancestors—Tsuda, Sode, and Anemaro; my parents of seven generations past and those currently living; my six kinds of relatives; and all sentient beings throughout the boundless Dharma-realm.
